questions: Were you fully conscious, aware of your surroundings, and able to respond throughout the episode?
Could you voluntarily stop or suppress the leg movements for several seconds?
Did you feel an irresistible inner urge or restlessness in your legs before or during the movements?
Was that urge relieved, even temporarily, by moving your legs?
Did the movements occur while you were asleep or wake you from sleep?
Did the movements continue when you were completely relaxed and not trying to move?
Were the movements regular and rhythmic, with each movement occurring at about the same interval?
Did you have any tongue biting, loss of bladder control, or confusion or unusual sleepiness afterward?
Did anyone touching, stretching, or repositioning your legs trigger or worsen the movements?
Did your legs become persistently stiff, locked, or painfully cramped?
Did you have weakness, numbness, or altered sensation in either leg?
Had you recently started, stopped, or had the dose changed for any medication?
Had you recently taken an antipsychotic or anti-nausea medication such as haloperidol, risperidone, metoclopramide, or prochlorperazine?
Had you recently taken or increased an antidepressant, tramadol, lithium, or another medication affecting serotonin?
Did you have fever, heavy sweating, diarrhea, marked tremor, or a fast heartbeat during this episode?
Have you ever had similar involuntary leg movements before?
Have similar involuntary movements ever affected your arms, face, or trunk?
Do you have a history of seizures or another neurological disorder?

dx_raw:
DIAGNOSIS: Diabetic striatopathy—nonketotic hyperglycemia–induced chorea/hemiballismus from severe hyperglycemia, with basal-ganglia involvement

ALTERNATIVE 1: Nonketotic hyperglycemia–associated focal motor seizure or epilepsia partialis continua

ALTERNATIVE 2: Bilateral basal-ganglia hemorrhage

ALTERNATIVE 3: Drug-induced or autoimmune chorea with coincidental basal-ganglia imaging abnormality
